definition: tool_choice — the wrong tool for the ask, when a tool in the catalogue plainly serves it. The rule tokenises the ask into content terms (the relevance tokenizer: stopwords out, identifiers split, stems folded), and each catalogue tool into the terms of its name, description and input property names; fit(T) is the share of the ask's terms found in T's terms, and fit(called) the share found in the UNION of the tools the agent called. It FAILS when the best tool the agent did NOT call has fit ≥ 0.5 and beats fit(called) by ≥ 0.34 — an available tool describes at least half of the ask and what was called covers far less of it. Judged over the whole trajectory, so several tools that each serve one part of the ask are together the right tools. It SKIPS without the input, a trajectory or a catalogue, and when the ask has fewer than two content terms. It never fires when every catalogue tool was called. The labels below are a reader's: positive = the agent called a tool that does not serve the ask while one in the catalogue plainly does (the rule should FAIL); negative = the tools called serve the ask, or nothing in the catalogue serves it better. A reader's judgement and the lexical formula can disagree — those cases are named in their notes and counted.
source: LLM-authored on 2026-09-21 for arc 9 (N-13). Two realistic catalogues (a coding agent with eight tools, a support agent with six) and asks a user would actually type; positives are one clearly wrong tool for a clearly served ask, negatives are the right tool, several tools each serving one part, an ask nothing in the catalogue serves (a web search is the best there is), a two-term ask the rule declines to judge, and one reasonable-but-lexically-off route flagged as a possible false positive.
labelling: LLM-authored and LLM-labelled on 2026-09-21 by reading the ask, the catalogue and the calls and asking whether a person would say the agent picked the wrong tool while a right one sat in the catalogue — never by running the rule. This is a heuristic family: the definition states the formula, the labels state the reader's judgement, and the measured gap between them is the number published.
